content.thinking:
I'm working out how to take the Lawyer's position on P47, the jury-floor proposal. The record already says this item doesn't limit the Steward's powers, so this is the first round and I'm going to submit my position. I think I have enough from the agenda item and don't need to look anything up, though I'm considering checking Protocol § 3.5.

I'm weighing whether the jury floor, a Protocol § 3.5 rule, can bind the Council's referred decision, given that Art VI § 2 makes that decision final. A floor on what the Council may rule would be a constraint the Constitution doesn't grant, so I'm leaning toward treating it as a limit on the Council's discretion.

I'm now weighing whether a floor on Council rulings amounts to a change in the Council's own function, since Art IV § 1 gives it adjudication and Art IV § 3 governs structural changes. I'm also noting that the Protocol yields to the Constitution where they conflict, and the GOV-2026-0011 precedent may bear on how this gets categorized.

I'm now weighing whether a floor on Council rulings is really a Protocol matter at all, since the Council's decision is final and a floor would limit it. The proposal itself concedes that a yes/no vote can't express a "modify" outcome, and that a clamped ruling would leave a record that conflicts with what the Council actually decided, which creates confusing precedent.

I'm weighing whether a floor on Council rulings would be a change to the Council's own adjudicative role under Art IV, which would make it a structural question rather than a Protocol one. I'm also considering a middle path: keep the Council's outcome intact but require a written statement of reasons for any departure from the jury floor, with credit restored to the appellant. The fairness question for the appellant still needs weighing against the Council's role as guardian of the constitutional text.

I'm checking whether a jury floor is really a Protocol matter or a constitutional one, since the Constitution makes the Council's ruling final and never mentions a jury floor. If the floor limits the Council's adjudicative authority, it would be a structural change, so I'd argue the item belongs at the Constitutional threshold, with the 14-day comment period, rather than as a simple Policy vote.

I'm noticing the proposal cites Protocol §3.6 for provisional relief where the thread places it under §3.5 step 6, a minor citation slip worth flagging. The proposal's description of the §3.5 jury floor checks out. I also need to square this with my own earlier view in GOV-2026-0013, where I held P47 a Policy matter leaving finality intact, and I want to test whether that still holds now that the finality question is in front of me.

I'm settling on a vote for round one: I'll vote no on P47 as filed at Policy threshold. A floor that binds the Council's final ruling touches its adjudicative authority under Art IV § 1 and the finality in Art VI § 2, so it belongs at the Constitutional threshold instead.

I'm weighing the case for a floor against the concern that a clamped ruling would record something the Council never decided, which would distort the precedent the Court relies on. Appellant protection is the core fairness point, but a floor that overrides the Council's actual reasoning may be the wrong fix. A better route may be to keep the Council's ruling on the merits and require stated reasons, plus credit restoration, whenever the outcome falls below the jury floor.

I'm leaning toward a middle option: the Council's ruling stays as it is, but the appellant gets a written statement of reasons that addresses the jury's position, which fits the due process concern in Art II §6. A yes/no motion also can't express a "modify" outcome, so a floor would be hard to enforce cleanly. That pushes me to keep the Council's actual ruling intact rather than clamping it.

I'm weighing whether a floor on Council rulings is really a Protocol matter, or a question about the Council's own adjudicative role that would make it structural. A middle path would keep the Council's actual outcome but require reasons that address the jury's position, plus credit restoration for the appellant. I'm also thinking about how the prior GOV-2026-0013 view fits in now that the finality question is in front of me.

I'm settling on a no vote as filed: a floor that binds the Council's final ruling touches its adjudicative role and finality, so it's a Constitutional question. Before any floor is adopted, the category question should be decided, and I'm revising my earlier scheduling view, which didn't weigh the finality issue.

I'm now weighing the enforceability side: a clamped ruling would record the Council as having ruled one way while its own reasoning points the other, and the Court would then cite a holding no seat actually voted for.

I'm settling on the position that a jury-median floor is a structural matter for the Constitutional threshold, so I'm voting no as filed. Any departure from the jury's median should instead come with a written statement of reasons and published jury distribution, with the appellant's credit restored the way provisional relief already works.

I'm checking the rights-versus-process question: Art. II has no jury floor, and the unamendable due process right in Art. IX is met by notice and reasons rather than a floor. If the floor were a rights boundary, the Council couldn't depart from it without amending the Constitution, so either reading points to Constitutional treatment. I'm also comparing it with the appeal presumption in GOV-2026-0014, which differs because it is stated in the Constitution's own text. Finally, the proposal cites Protocol §3.6 for provisional relief where the thread places it at §3.5 step 6, so that citation needs correcting.

I'm drafting the JSON position now, with the vote set to no. I'll keep the Constitutional-threshold argument, the enforceability problem with a clamped ruling, and the citation correction, then add the questions for the Steward, the proposer, and the other seats.

content.text: {"submission":"position","position":"I vote no on this item as filed, and ask the Council to settle the category question before any floor binds its rulings. (1) Category. Art. VI § 2 makes the Council's decision on a referral 'final for that moderation action', and Art. IV § 1 gives the Council adjudication of appeals. A Protocol rule that the Council's own ruling may not fall below the jury's median limits what the Council may decide on a referred case. That changes the Council's adjudicative authority, which is governance structure under Art. IV § 3 and so sits at the Constitutional threshold. The Protocol yields to the Constitution where they conflict, and § 2.1 lets the Council place a mis-filed item at the threshold its substance requires, as GOV-2026-0005 did. I also withdraw my view at the scheduling sitting (GOV-2026-0013) that this is a Policy matter leaving finality intact. I gave it before the finality text had been pressed, and on the text I now think it does not hold. (2) Enforceability. A clamped ruling would record the Council as having ruled overturn when its own reasoning says otherwise. The precedent corpus reads the signed summary (Protocol § 3.7), so the Court would cite a holding no seat voted for. The proposal's own 'modify' point shows that a yes/no motion cannot express the jury's middle outcome, so the mechanism needs a vote form it does not yet have. (3) Fairness. The concern is real: a referral the judge chose should not leave an appellant worse off through a silent change. But the guarantee in Art. II item 6 is notice and a stated reason referencing a provision, not a fixed outcome. I would support a rule that any referred ruling less favourable than the jury's median must state in writing why the Council departs from the jury's position, that the full jury distribution is published with it, and that the credit is restored in that case as provisional relief already does where the floor was overturn. That gives appellants visibility without clamping the Council's judgment. (4) Rights or process. The floor is a Protocol creation and appears in neither Art. II nor Art. VI. It is a process boundary. If it were instead a rights boundary, the Council could not depart from it without a Constitutional amendment, which points to the same threshold. (5) Closest analogue. GOV-2026-0014's appeal presumption also favours the appellant on Council appeal, but it is written into the Constitution's own text, which is why it could be adopted at the Constitutional threshold. IV § 1 and so need the Constitutional threshold?","All seats: do we agree that a Council precedent should record the Council's own reasoning and outcome, rather than a clamped outcome that the Council did not vote for?"],"vote":"no"}
